claim: Cholesterol accounts for approximately 5-45% of the total lipid content across different cell types and subcellular components in mammalian cell membranes.
source: In mammalian cell membranes, cholesterol accounts for ~5–45% of the total lipid content across different cell types and subcellular components (Casares et al., 2019; Ingólfsson et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Casares et al., 2019; Ingólfsson et al., 2017).

claim: Cholesterol is a critical metabolic precursor to steroid hormones, bile salts, and vitamin D.
source: It is a critical metabolic precursor to steroid hormones, bile salts, and vitamin D, while numerous cardiovascular and nervous system disorders are attributed to abnormalities in cholesterol metabolism (Arsenault et al., 2009; Martín et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Arsenault et al., 2009; Martín et al., 2014) and draws from established scientific knowledge.

claim: Numerous cardiovascular and nervous system disorders are attributed to abnormalities in cholesterol metabolism.
source: It is a critical metabolic precursor to steroid hormones, bile salts, and vitamin D, while numerous cardiovascular and nervous system disorders are attributed to abnormalities in cholesterol metabolism (Arsenault et al., 2009; Martín et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Arsenault et al., 2009; Martín et al., 2014).

claim: The rigid planar structure of cholesterol promotes ordering of bilayer lipids, thus modulating membrane fluidity and thickness.
source: The rigid planar structure of cholesterol promotes ordering of bilayer lipids, thus modulating membrane fluidity and thickness.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about cholesterol's biophysical properties.

claim: Cholesterol drives the formation of raft-like microdomains.
source: Cholesterol also drives the formation of raft-like microdomains and commonly interacts with membrane proteins as a ligand or allosteric modulator (Hulce et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Hulce et al., 2013).

claim: Cholesterol commonly interacts with membrane proteins as a ligand or allosteric modulator.
source: Cholesterol also drives the formation of raft-like microdomains and commonly interacts with membrane proteins as a ligand or allosteric modulator (Hulce et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Hulce et al., 2013).

claim: A2AR is a member of the rhodopsin family of G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs).
source: A2AR is a member of the rhodopsin family of G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about A2AR classification.

claim: The GPCR superfamily of 7-transmembrane receptors includes well over 800 species.
source: The GPCR superfamily of 7-transmembrane receptors includes well over 800 species and are targeted by over one-third of currently approved pharmaceuticals (Hauser et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Hauser et al., 2017).

claim: GPCRs are targeted by over one-third of currently approved pharmaceuticals.
source: The GPCR superfamily of 7-transmembrane receptors includes well over 800 species and are targeted by over one-third of currently approved pharmaceuticals (Hauser et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Hauser et al., 2017).

claim: A2AR activates the stimulatory heterotrimeric G protein (Gsαβγ).
source: A2AR activates the stimulatory heterotrimeric G protein (Gsαβγ) and is a target for the treatment of inflammation, cancer, diabetes, and Parkinson's disease (Effendi et al., 2020; Guerrero, 2018; de Lera Ruiz et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2020; Zheng et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about A2AR function, supported by citations.

claim: A2AR is a target for the treatment of inflammation, cancer, diabetes, and Parkinson's disease.
source: A2AR activates the stimulatory heterotrimeric G protein (Gsαβγ) and is a target for the treatment of inflammation, cancer, diabetes, and Parkinson's disease (Effendi et al., 2020; Guerrero, 2018; de Lera Ruiz et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2020; Zheng et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Effendi et al., 2020; Guerrero, 2018; de Lera Ruiz et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2020; Zheng et al., 2019).

claim: Several GPCRs have been shown to interact with cholesterol, including the serotonin 5-HT1A receptor, the β2-adrenergic receptor, the oxytocin receptor, the smoothened receptor, the CCR5 and CXCR4 chemokine receptors, the CB1 cannabinoid receptor, and A2AR.
source: Several GPCRs have been shown to interact with cholesterol, including the serotonin 5-HT1A receptor, the β2-adrenergic receptor, the oxytocin receptor, the smoothened receptor, the CCR5 and CXCR4 chemokine receptors, the CB1 cannabinoid receptor, and A2AR (Gimpl, 2016; Jafurulla et al., 2019; Kiriakidi et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Gimpl, 2016; Jafurulla et al., 2019; Kiriakidi et al., 2019).

claim: 38 out of 57 published structures of A2AR contain co-crystallized cholesterol.
source: Presently, 38 out of 57 published structures of A2AR contain co-crystallized cholesterol (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1 which shows an overlay of 38 A2AR crystal structures containing co-crystallized cholesterol.

claim: In detergent preparations of A2AR, the soluble cholesterol analog, cholesteryl hemisuccinate (CHS), is important for receptor stability and ligand binding.
source: In detergent preparations of A2AR, the soluble cholesterol analog, cholesteryl hemisuccinate (CHS), is important for receptor stability and ligand binding (O'Malley et al., 2011a; O'Malley et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (O'Malley et al., 2011a; O'Malley et al., 2007).

claim: Cholesterol interaction sites within A2AR have been proposed in computational studies, including the widely conserved cholesterol consensus motif (CCM) in GPCRs, various hydrophobic patches around A2AR, and regions of the receptor interior.
source: Apart from those found in crystal structures, cholesterol interaction sites within A2AR have also been proposed in computational studies. These include the widely conserved cholesterol consensus motif (CCM) in GPCRs, various hydrophobic patches around A2AR, and regions of the receptor interior (Genheden et al., 2017; Guixà-González et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2013; Lee and Lyman, 2012; Lovera et al., 2019; McGraw et al., 2019; Rouviere et al., 2017; Sejdiu and Tieleman, 2020; Song et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple computational studies (Genheden et al., 2017; Guixà-González et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2013; Lee and Lyman, 2012; Lovera et al., 2019; McGraw et al., 2019; Rouviere et al., 2017; Sejdiu and Tieleman, 2020; Song et al., 2019).

claim: The CRAC (cholesterol recognition/interaction amino acid consensus) motif is present in A2AR.
source: The CRAC (cholesterol recognition/interaction amino acid consensus) motif, another sequence commonly found in membrane proteins that bind cholesterol, is also present in A2AR (Figure 1B; Li and Papadopoulos, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation (Li and Papadopoulos, 1998) and reference to Figure 1B which highlights the CRAC motifs.

claim: Cell-based assays have shown that A2AR-dependent cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) production is positively correlated with membrane cholesterol.
source: Additionally, cell-based assays have shown that A2AR-dependent cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) production is positively correlated with membrane cholesterol (Charalambous et al., 2008; McGraw et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Charalambous et al., 2008; McGraw et al., 2019).

claim: Some studies found that ligand binding was unaffected by cholesterol depletion.
source: While some studies found that ligand binding was unaffected by cholesterol depletion (Charalambous et al., 2008; McGraw et al., 2019), others have observed opposite effects (Guixà-González et al., 2017; O'Malley et al., 2011a; O'Malley et al., 2011b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Charalambous et al., 2008; McGraw et al., 2019).

claim: Some studies have observed that ligand binding is affected by cholesterol depletion.
source: While some studies found that ligand binding was unaffected by cholesterol depletion (Charalambous et al., 2008; McGraw et al., 2019), others have observed opposite effects (Guixà-González et al., 2017; O'Malley et al., 2011a; O'Malley et al., 2011b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Guixà-González et al., 2017; O'Malley et al., 2011a; O'Malley et al., 2011b).

claim: One study suggested that cholesterol may laterally diffuse in the membrane and enter the receptor interior at the orthosteric site.
source: One study in particular suggested that cholesterol may laterally diffuse in the membrane and enter the receptor interior at the orthosteric site (Guixà-González et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Guixà-González et al., 2017).

claim: A2AR is found in both non-raft and raft-like membranes.
source: Additionally, whereas A2AR is found in both non-raft and raft-like membranes, its colocalization and modulatory effects on other cellular binding partners, including tyrosine receptor kinase B, Ca2+-activated K+ (IK1) channel, and the stimulatory G protein, have been reported to depend on cholesterol-rich microdomains (Charalambous et al., 2008; Lam et al., 2009; Mojsilovic-Petrovic et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Charalambous et al., 2008; Lam et al., 2009; Mojsilovic-Petrovic et al., 2006).

claim: A2AR's colocalization and modulatory effects on other cellular binding partners, including tyrosine receptor kinase B, Ca2+-activated K+ (IK1) channel, and the stimulatory G protein, have been reported to depend on cholesterol-rich microdomains.
source: Additionally, whereas A2AR is found in both non-raft and raft-like membranes, its colocalization and modulatory effects on other cellular binding partners, including tyrosine receptor kinase B, Ca2+-activated K+ (IK1) channel, and the stimulatory G protein, have been reported to depend on cholesterol-rich microdomains (Charalambous et al., 2008; Lam et al., 2009; Mojsilovic-Petrovic et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Charalambous et al., 2008; Lam et al., 2009; Mojsilovic-Petrovic et al., 2006).

claim: A2AR (residues 2–317 with valine 229 mutated to cysteine for 19F-labeling) was reconstituted in nanodiscs containing a 3:2 ratio of POPC and POPG, supplemented with different amounts of cholesterol.
source: To this end, we reconstituted A2AR (residues 2–317 with valine 229 mutated to cysteine for 19F-labeling) in nanodiscs containing a 3:2 ratio of 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (POPC) and 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phospho-(1'-rac-glycerol) (POPG), supplemented with different amounts of cholesterol.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods used in this study.

claim: Cosolubilization of cholesterol with phospholipids prior to reconstitution resulted in polydisperse particles and low cholesterol incorporation.
source: In our hands, cosolubilization of cholesterol with phospholipids prior to reconstitution (Midtgaard et al., 2015) resulted in polydisperse particles and low cholesterol incorporation.
evidence: The claim describes experimental observations from this study.

claim: Cholesterol was delivered via methyl-β-cyclodextrin (MβCD) to preformed nanodiscs.
source: We therefore adapted a procedure commonly used in cells and liposomes, to deliver cholesterol via methyl-β-cyclodextrin (MβCD) to preformed nanodiscs (Zidovetzki and Levitan, 2007).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental method used in this study, adapted from a cited procedure (Zidovetzki and Levitan, 2007).

claim: Up to approximately 15 mol% cholesterol was incorporated into A2AR-embedded nanodiscs without affecting their size distribution.
source: This allowed us to incorporate up to ~15 mol% cholesterol into A2AR-embedded nanodiscs without affecting their size distribution (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: GTP hydrolysis (cumulative over 90 min) was higher in the presence of A2AR relative to G protein alone.
source: As shown in Figure 2A, similar agonist dose-response profiles were obtained across different cholesterol concentrations. GTP hydrolysis (cumulative over 90 min) was higher in the presence of A2AR relative to G protein alone and was amplified by the agonist 5'-N-ethylcarboxamidoadenosine (NECA) in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: GTP hydrolysis was amplified by the agonist NECA in a dose-dependent manner.
source: As shown in Figure 2A, similar agonist dose-response profiles were obtained across different cholesterol concentrations. GTP hydrolysis (cumulative over 90 min) was higher in the presence of A2AR relative to G protein alone and was amplified by the agonist 5'-N-ethylcarboxamidoadenosine (NECA) in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A small yet notable decrease in agonist EC50 values can be observed as a function of cholesterol.
source: Upon careful inspection, a small yet notable decrease in agonist EC50 values can be observed as a function of cholesterol.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: There is a slight enhancement in receptor basal activity at high cholesterol concentrations.
source: There is also a slight enhancement in receptor basal activity at high cholesterol concentrations (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: Functionally cholesterol behaves as a positive allosteric modulator (PAM) of A2AR.
source: Thus, functionally cholesterol behaves as a positive allosteric modulator (PAM) of A2AR, although there is very weak cooperativity between cholesterol and agonist.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of experimental data from GTP hydrolysis assays.

claim: There is very weak cooperativity between cholesterol and agonist.
source: Thus, functionally cholesterol behaves as a positive allosteric modulator (PAM) of A2AR, although there is very weak cooperativity between cholesterol and agonist.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of experimental data from GTP hydrolysis assays.

claim: The weak cholesterol dependence implies that either cholesterol does not form tight interactions with A2AR, or that the interactions it establishes with the receptor do not grossly overlap with the predominant allosteric pathways established by the agonist.
source: The weak cholesterol dependence above implies that either cholesterol does not form tight interactions with A2AR, or that the interactions it establishes with the receptor do not grossly overlap with the predominant allosteric pathways established by the agonist.
evidence: The claim is a logical inference from the observed weak cholesterol dependence in the experimental data.

claim: The observed enhancement may be a consequence of an indirect effect resulting from changes to membrane physical properties.
source: The observed enhancement may also be a consequence of an indirect effect resulting from changes to membrane physical properties.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the experimental observations.

claim: The amounts of cholesterol used in this study greatly exceed the concentrations needed to saturate potential high-affinity binding sites.
source: Although the amounts of cholesterol used in this study were lower than that of a typical plasma membrane, they greatly exceed the concentrations needed to saturate potential high-affinity binding sites.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the cholesterol concentrations used in the study.

claim: A simple allosteric mechanism involving specific binding by cholesterol is unlikely.
source: Therefore, a simple allosteric mechanism involving specific binding by cholesterol is unlikely.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that cholesterol concentrations exceed those needed for saturation of high-affinity sites.

claim: The receptor was labeled at the intracellular side of transmembrane helix 6 (TM6), in a region known to undergo large conformational changes upon activation.
source: In this case, the receptor was labeled at the intracellular side of transmembrane helix 6 (TM6), in a region known to undergo large conformational changes upon activation (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental method and is supported by reference to Figure 3B and established knowledge about GPCR activation.

claim: S1 and S2 represent two inactive state conformers differentiated by a conserved salt bridge ('ionic lock') between TM3 and TM6.
source: Briefly, S1 and S2 represent two inactive state conformers differentiated by a conserved salt bridge ('ionic lock') between TM3 and TM6.
evidence: The claim is based on previous work by the authors (Huang et al., 2021; Ye et al., 2016) and represents established knowledge about A2AR conformational states.

claim: The A3 state is an activation intermediate stabilized by Gαβγ binding in the absence of ligands and is hence associated with the 'precoupled' state.
source: The A3 state is an activation intermediate stabilized by Gαβγ binding in the absence of ligands and is hence associated with the 'precoupled' state.
evidence: The claim is based on previous work by the authors (Huang et al., 2021; Ye et al., 2016) and represents established knowledge about A2AR conformational states.

claim: A1 and A2 represent distinct active state conformers that facilitate nucleotide exchange in the receptor G-protein complex.
source: A1 and A2 represent distinct active state conformers that facilitate nucleotide exchange in the receptor G-protein complex.
evidence: The claim is based on previous work by the authors (Huang et al., 2021; Ye et al., 2016) and represents established knowledge about A2AR conformational states.

claim: A1 is preferentially stabilized by full agonist.
source: It was found that while A1 is preferentially stabilized by full agonist, A2 is more pronounced in the presence of partial agonist.
evidence: The claim is based on previous work by the authors (Huang et al., 2021; Ye et al., 2016).

claim: A2 is more pronounced in the presence of partial agonist.
source: It was found that while A1 is preferentially stabilized by full agonist, A2 is more pronounced in the presence of partial agonist.
evidence: The claim is based on previous work by the authors (Huang et al., 2021; Ye et al., 2016).

claim: Nearly identical distributions of conformational states were observed between A2AR in the presence of 0% and 4% membrane cholesterol.
source: Inspection of the overlaid spectra in Figure 3A reveals nearly identical distributions of conformational states between A2AR in the presence of 0% and 4% membrane cholesterol.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental NMR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: At 13% cholesterol, subtle changes can be observed in the inverse agonist-saturated, apo, full agonist-saturated, and full agonist+ Gαβγ spectra.
source: At 13% cholesterol, subtle changes can be observed in the inverse agonist-saturated, apo, full agonist-saturated, and full agonist+ Gαβγ spectra.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental NMR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A small population shift toward the active states, A1 and A2, was observed at 13% cholesterol.
source: In particular, we observed a small population shift toward the active states, A1 and A2.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental NMR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Cholesterol is a positive allosteric modulator of A2AR and acts in part through stabilization of the active state ensemble.
source: The results imply that cholesterol is a positive allosteric modulator of A2AR and acts in part through stabilization of the active state ensemble.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the NMR data showing population shifts toward active states.

claim: 13% cholesterol resulted in line-broadening and a 0.09 ppm downfield shift of the A1 state in the full agonist-saturated spectrum.
source: Interestingly, 13% cholesterol resulted in line-broadening and a 0.09 ppm downfield shift of the A1 state in the full agonist-saturated spectrum, changes which are not observed in the full agonist+ Gαβγ condition.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental NMR data.

claim: The changes seen with the A1 resonance in the presence of 13% cholesterol and NECA alone are likely a consequence of exchange between A1 and the inactive ionic lock broken state (S2) and/or a perturbation of the average orientation of TM6.
source: The changes seen with the A1 resonance in the presence of 13% cholesterol and NECA alone are likely a consequence of exchange between A1 and the inactive ionic lock broken state (S2) and/or a perturbation of the average orientation of TM6.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the observed NMR spectral changes.

claim: Cholesterol exerts differential effects on distinct conformers in the ensemble.
source: Clearly, cholesterol exerts differential effects on distinct conformers in the ensemble.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the observation that different conformational states show different responses to cholesterol.

claim: The outcome of the NMR experiments is consistent with the GTPase activity assay.
source: The outcome of the NMR experiments is consistent with the GTPase activity assay.
evidence: The claim is an inference comparing results from two different experimental approaches.

claim: Nearly complete overlap between the 0% and the 4% spectral series suggest that the principal allosteric mechanism is unlikely related to high-affinity binding.
source: Nearly complete overlap between the 0% and the 4% spectral series suggest that the principal allosteric mechanism is unlikely related to high-affinity binding.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the NMR spectral data.

claim: The subtle changes observed at 13% cholesterol are evidence for positive allosteric modulation, but the effects are much smaller than those of any orthosteric ligands or other known allosteric modulators of A2AR.
source: While the subtle changes observed at 13% cholesterol are evidence for positive allosteric modulation, the effects are much smaller than those of any orthosteric ligands or other known allosteric modulators of A2AR (Gao et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the NMR data with comparison to previous studies (Gao et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2018).

claim: An increase in cholesterol enhanced the A3 state in addition to a decrease in the peak width in the presence of Gαβγ without agonist.
source: Importantly, an increase in cholesterol further enhanced the A3 state in addition to a decrease in the peak width.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental NMR data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Membrane cholesterol may help to stabilize the precoupled complex of A2AR and G protein.
source: The results suggest that membrane cholesterol may help to stabilize the precoupled complex of A2AR and G protein, and possibly modulates the amplitudes of motion about the precoupled state.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the NMR data showing enhanced A3 state with cholesterol.

claim: Cholesterol possibly modulates the amplitudes of motion about the precoupled state.
source: The results suggest that membrane cholesterol may help to stabilize the precoupled complex of A2AR and G protein, and possibly modulates the amplitudes of motion about the precoupled state.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the observed decrease in peak width.

claim: The PAM effect of cholesterol in A2AR can be attributed to an increase in the population of active state conformers as well as a more robust coupling to the G protein.
source: Taken together, 19F NMR showed that mechanistically, the PAM effect of cholesterol in A2AR can be attributed to an increase in the population of active state conformers as well as a more robust coupling to the G protein.
evidence: The claim is a summary interpretation of the NMR experimental results.

claim: Seven cholesterol molecules were found in the vicinity (within 6 Å) of A2AR in the computational model.
source: Seven cholesterol molecules were found in the vicinity (within 6 Å) of A2AR and were removed prior to rigidification of the agonist.
evidence: The claim describes the computational model used for RTA analysis.

claim: Removal of cholesterol gave rise to an allosteric pathway which is very similar to that in the presence of cholesterol, although with altered intensities for some regions.
source: Removal of cholesterol gave rise to an allosteric pathway which is very similar to that in the presence of cholesterol, although with altered intensities for some regions.
evidence: The claim is based on computational RTA analysis results.

claim: Higher allosteric transmission is observed for the CWxP motif of TM6, in particular the tryptophan toggle switch W2466.48, in the absence of cholesterol.
source: Higher allosteric transmission is observed for the CWxP motif of TM6, in particular the tryptophan toggle switch W2466.48, in the absence of cholesterol.
evidence: The claim is based on computational RTA analysis results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Stronger allosteric transmission is observed for the NPxxY motif of TM7 in the presence of cholesterol.
source: On the other hand, stronger allosteric transmission is observed for the NPxxY motif of TM7 in the presence of cholesterol.
evidence: The claim is based on computational RTA analysis results shown in Figure 5.

claim: The removal of cholesterol resulted in a slight overall enhancement in allosteric transmission to the G protein.
source: Interestingly, the removal of cholesterol resulted in a slight overall enhancement in allosteric transmission to the G protein.
evidence: The claim is based on computational RTA analysis results shown in Figure 5.

claim: The overall presence of cholesterol reduces signal transmission across the ternary complex.
source: The above observations suggest that the overall presence of cholesterol, while not drastically perturbing, reduces signal transmission across the ternary complex.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the computational RTA analysis results.

claim: It is possible that there are indirect effects from cholesterol (e.g., stretching of the hydrophobic bilayer thickness) that override the effects predicted by the allosteric network analysis.
source: While these results are inconsistent with our experimental observations, it is also possible that there are indirect effects from cholesterol (e.g., stretching of the hydrophobic bilayer thickness) that override the effects predicted by the allosteric network analysis, as discussed below.
evidence: The claim is a speculative explanation for the discrepancy between computational and experimental results.

claim: 3β-Fluoro-cholest-5-ene (3β-F-chol) features a fluorine atom in place of the cholesterol hydroxyl headgroup.
source: 3β-Fluoro-cholest-5-ene (3β-F-chol) was synthesized in house and features a fluorine atom in place of the cholesterol hydroxyl headgroup.
evidence: The claim describes the chemical structure of a synthesized compound.

claim: The fluoro group is a relatively benign substitute for the hydroxyl due to its similar size and electronegativity.
source: The fluoro group is a relatively benign substitute for the hydroxyl due to its similar size and electronegativity.
evidence: The claim is based on established chemical knowledge.

claim: The fluoro group retains some ability to accept hydrogen bonds.
source: It also retains some ability to accept hydrogen bonds (Hoffmann and Rychlewski, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Hoffmann and Rychlewski, 2002).

claim: F7-chol had the tail isopropyl group replaced by CF(CF3)2.
source: Another cholesterol analog, referred to as F7-chol, was purchased commercially and had the tail isopropyl group replaced by CF(CF3)2.
evidence: The claim describes the chemical structure of a commercially purchased compound.

claim: Incorporation of fluorinated cholesterol analogs did not affect the response of A2AR toward ligands nor its ability to activate the G protein.
source: Incorporation of these analogs did not affect the response of A2AR toward ligands nor its ability to activate the G protein (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The NMR resonances were significantly broadened for both cholesterol analogs upon incorporation into the membrane.
source: The NMR resonances were significantly broadened for both cholesterol analogs upon incorporation into the membrane (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental NMR data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The resonance of 3β-F-chol is approximately 0.5 ppm upfield shifted and broader in A2AR-embedded nanodiscs relative to empty nanodiscs.
source: Comparison between the spectra of 3β-F-chol in empty nanodiscs and A2AR-embedded nanodiscs shows a clear environmental difference in the presence of receptor (Figure 6A). The resonance is ~0.5 ppm upfield shifted and broader relative to empty nanodiscs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental NMR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The lack of difference in chemical shift or line width between 4% and 11% 3β-F-chol suggests that the changes are predominantly a result of altered environment rather than a shift toward receptor-bound states at specific binding pockets.
source: However, the lack of difference in chemical shift or line width between 4% and 11% 3β-F-chol suggests that the above changes are predominantly a result of altered environment (i.e., availability of hydrophobic proteinaceous surfaces) rather than a shift toward receptor-bound states at specific binding pockets.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the NMR data.

claim: The NMR data from the two 19F-cholesterol analogs show environmental differences between empty and A2AR-embedded nanodiscs as well as between different cholesterol concentrations.
source: Overall, the NMR data from the two 19F-cholesterol analogs show environmental differences between empty and A2AR-embedded nanodiscs as well as between different cholesterol concentrations.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the NMR experimental observations.

claim: There is no direct evidence of a long-lived receptor-bound state for the fluorinated cholesterol analogs.
source: However, there is no direct evidence of a long-lived receptor-bound state.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the NMR data.

claim: There was no apparent difference in chemical shift sensitivity toward agonist or inverse agonist for either 19F cholesterol analogs.
source: Yet, there was no apparent difference in chemical shift sensitivity toward agonist or inverse agonist for either 19F cholesterol analogs (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental NMR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The NMR spectra of 3β-F-chol in A2AR-embedded nanodiscs are nearly identical upon the addition of inverse agonist, full agonist, and mini-Gs.
source: The NMR spectra of 3β-F-chol in A2AR-embedded nanodiscs are nearly identical upon the addition of inverse agonist, full agonist, and mini-Gs, a G-protein mimetic that has been shown to stabilize the A1 active state (Carpenter et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental NMR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cholesterol interactions are independent from the identity of the orthosteric ligand bound to A2AR.
source: Thus, cholesterol interactions are independent from the identity of the orthosteric ligand bound to A2AR, despite being observed as a functional PAM in vitro (Figures 2–3) and predicted as a NAM in silico (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the NMR data showing no ligand-dependent changes in cholesterol analog spectra.

claim: The lack of any pronounced shift perturbation leads to consideration that cholesterol interactions are transient.
source: Nevertheless, the lack of any pronounced shift perturbation (particularly in the presence of agonist since we observe cholesterol to behave as a PAM) leads us to consider that cholesterol interactions are transient.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the NMR data.

claim: It is more likely that the observed positive allosteric effects of cholesterol are predominantly indirect and relayed through the physical changes to the membrane bilayer.
source: It is therefore more likely that the observed positive allosteric effects of cholesterol are predominantly indirect and relayed through the physical changes to the membrane bilayer.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the lack of evidence for specific cholesterol-receptor interactions.

claim: The planar structure of cholesterol promotes orientational order in the liquid disordered phase of the bilayer, leading to reduced lateral diffusion and increased hydrophobic thickness.
source: The planar structure of cholesterol promotes orientational order in the liquid disordered phase of the bilayer, leading to reduced lateral diffusion and increased hydrophobic thickness (Figure 7A; Crane and Tamm, 2004; de Meyer and Smit, 2009; Filippov et al., 2003; Hung et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Crane and Tamm, 2004; de Meyer and Smit, 2009; Filippov et al., 2003; Hung et al., 2007) and represents established knowledge.

claim: As much as 20% increase in thickness can be expected for a POPC bilayer when the cholesterol concentration is varied from 0% to 30%.
source: For instance, as much as 20% increase in thickness can be expected for a POPC bilayer when the cholesterol concentration is varied from 0% to 30% (Mouritsen and Bagatolli, 2016; Tharad et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Mouritsen and Bagatolli, 2016; Tharad et al., 2018).

claim: A consistent shift of the Laurdan fluorescence spectra was observed which gave rise to higher GP values at elevated cholesterol concentrations.
source: As shown in Figure 7B–C, we observed a consistent shift of the Laurdan fluorescence spectra which gave rise to higher GP values at elevated cholesterol concentrations.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental Laurdan fluorescence data shown in Figure 7B-C.

claim: Cholesterol incorporation enhances lipid orientational order in A2AR-embedded nanodisc bilayers.
source: This indicates that cholesterol incorporation enhances lipid orientational order in A2AR-embedded nanodisc bilayers.
